summary:
Tucumán stands under Argentina's national framework, and no Tucumán-specific rule material enough to depart from it is sourced here. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passing the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, permits a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval. An adult visitor's identity documents are therefore not gated by medical sign-off, and the United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That statutory position has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. A decree issued on 5 February 2025 restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the minors' measure illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene; the outcome of that litigation is not recorded in the sources available here.

Official hostility at federal level is documented. The government of President Javier Milei eliminated the federal Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry and dismissed trans employees hired under the Trans Labour Quota Law, which reserved at least 1% of public-sector jobs for trans people. Trans activists interviewed on 4 April 2025 described a chaotic and desperate situation with heightened exposure to violence, discrimination and poverty.

Violence risk is the sharper practical concern. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 bias-motivated crimes against LGBT people in Argentina during 2025, a record and an increase on 2024, averaging one every 38 hours; Agencia Presentes reported the figures on 19 March 2026. Trans women and travestis made up 62.5% of victims (142 cases), with 18 trans men targeted against 5 in 2024, alongside 13 lesbians and 4 non-binary people. Physical violence accounted for 64.8% of cases (147), and 32% occurred in police stations or penal institutions, with documented police involvement rising from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025.

Protection machinery is weak in practice. On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by an appeal court in 2020, so the gender-motivated aggravator does not apply in the case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
Argentina was the first country in Latin America to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protections exist through both national and provincial laws. An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 nonetheless records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration across the legal and civic environment a visitor enters.

Trans organisations named for Diana Sacayán, stabbed to death in 2015, and for Lohana Berkins reported in Washington Blade reporting of 10 April 2025 that the federal government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence. The national hate-crime monitoring body's 2025 figures were described by Agencia Presentes on 19 March 2026 as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

The province of Tucumán is treated here as one data point inside that national pattern: the decrees, the ministry's elimination and the hate-crime statistics are federal in scope and apply uniformly, while none of the sourced material documents Tucumán-specific policing, provincial prosecutions or provincial service provision.
localsOnly:
Residents employed in the public sector lost the protection of the Trans Labour Quota Law in practice when the federal government dismissed trans employees hired under it; the law's 1% reservation of public-sector jobs for trans people was the target of that action. The elimination of the federal Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry removed the institutional point of contact for gender and diversity policy that residents previously relied on.

Argentine residents seeking gender-affirming care for minors face the restrictions imposed by the decree of 5 February 2025, and trans people subject to the penal system are governed by the separate decree on prison housing. Both measures bind residents of Tucumán as they do those of every other province.

Legal gender change for adults remains administrative and medical-gatekeeping-free under Law 26.743, so residents can update national identity documents without surgery, hormone treatment or a court order.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tucumán-specific statute, provincial decree, court decision or enforcement record on legal gender recognition, facilities access or anti-discrimination complaint handling is sourced here, so the province-level position is unresolved rather than confirmed as identical to the national framework in every operational detail.

The litigation filed against the December- and February-stage executive measures on minors and on prison housing has no recorded outcome in the sources available here; whether the decree restricting gender-affirming care for minors remains fully in force, in whole or in part, is unresolved.

The 227 hate crimes recorded for 2025 are national totals with victim-type and setting breakdowns, but no provincial distribution of those cases is sourced, so Tucumán's share of the recorded violence is unresolved.

Whether the travesticidio aggravating circumstance is charged in other pending Argentine cases after the Supreme Court's ruling of 5 April 2025 is not sourced here.
